description: Terra Australis es un equipo multidisciplinario localizado en Argentina. Apasionado por la tecnología, la exploración espacial y el análisis de datos. Trabajaremos sobre el desafío “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS”.
summary:
Terra Australis is a web app that turns two decades of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burn-activity calendar for South America.

NASA's MODIS sensors have recorded active fires since 2000 and are now being replaced by VIIRS, which sees much smaller fires. If the two records are joined directly, the sensor change appears as a false increase: in our six-country test, raw VIIRS showed 3.6 times more activity than MODIS over the same fires. We built a harmonization pipeline that calibrates VIIRS to the MODIS scale. It uses the years when both sensors flew together and calibrates separately by region, month and day/night. It also removes non-vegetation heat sources and corrects for the small night fires that MODIS misses. In blind tests, the overall bias dropped from +262% to +0.05%.

Users can explore the harmonized series on an interactive map, compare any month with the historical median, and read an explanation at three levels: technical, general and for kids. A comparable record is what lets firefighters, land managers and researchers tell whether a fire season is truly unusual.
details:
Terra Australis has two parts: a data pipeline that harmonizes NASA FIRMS active fire detections from MODIS and VIIRS into a single scale, and a static web app that displays the result.

The pipeline runs in stages, from ingest to export:

  1. Common schema and filters. Both products are brought into one schema. It keeps only vegetation fires (type = 0) above a common confidence threshold and removes persistent industrial sources with a static mask.
  2. Clusters instead of pixels. Detections are grouped into H3 hexagonal cells, which reduces the resolution gap between the 1 km MODIS pixels and the 375 m VIIRS pixels.
  3. Night-time weighting. Each VIIRS night cluster is weighted by the probability that MODIS would have detected it given its fire radiative power. That probability is estimated against Aqua detections in the same cell and night.
  4. Calibration. Conversion factors (k) are computed over the 2018–2021 overlap. They are stratified by region, month, day/night and platform, with a hierarchical fallback and bootstrap uncertainty bands.
  5. Composition. The final series uses observed MODIS until 2021 and calibrated VIIRS from 2022 on. It distinguishes "no fire detected" from "no satellite coverage".

How we validated it

We used leave-one-year-out validation: each year of the overlap was hidden, estimated, and compared with what MODIS actually measured. The acceptance criteria are a yearly predicted/observed ratio between 0.9 and 1.1 and a yearly bias within ±10%. We also ran an ablation study comparing metrics and corrections. We document where the method still falls short, such as night-time 2020 in Argentina, linked to unusually intense fires in Córdoba.

The app

An interactive map shows harmonized activity per hexagon. Users can move through time by month or by 8-day window, see anomalies against the 2003–2021 median, and check which part of the series is observed and which part is estimated. A built-in explanation module presents the project at three levels: technical, general and for kids.

Impact

Around 95% of forest fires in Argentina are caused by people, and the fire season varies widely across South America. Prevention depends on knowing when and where fire is unusual. Without harmonization, every long-term trend that crosses the MODIS-to-VIIRS transition is biased upward. With it, firefighters can plan for critical months, and researchers can study how fire responds to climate and land use without mistaking a sensor change for a real trend.

Tools

Python, DuckDB, H3 and Parquet for the pipeline. JavaScript with Vite, MapLibre GL JS, deck.gl and h3-js for the web app. No backend: the app reads static JSON files generated by the pipeline.

Creativity and design factors

Instead of a black-box model, we chose a transparent ratio method that can be audited at every step and that reports its own uncertainty. Every run is tagged with a configuration hash so stale calibrations are never reused. We used a colorblind-safe palette (viridis) and clearly mark estimated values. We designed the explanation so that a jury member, a park ranger and a ten-year-old can each understand what the map shows and what it does not: a detection is not a confirmed fire, and a zero does not prove there was no fire.
